titel: Partnership, children and inheritance in the US
kurz: How couples split shared costs, how to save for children, and how inheritances and gifts are treated under US federal estate and gift tax and state law.

bloecke.md:
Money in a relationship is usually only discussed once something has gone wrong. Yet it comes down to three organisational and legal questions. What needs to be settled is who bears which share of the shared costs, who owns the money saved for children, and who decides and inherits if something happens to one of the partners.

All three questions can be answered in advance, usually in an afternoon. If they remain open, default rules apply: the intestacy law of your state, the account titles and the beneficiary forms you once filled in. These defaults are often tailored to a married couple with children together. For unmarried couples, blended families and couples living in different states over the years, they often lead to the wrong results.

## Splitting shared costs

There are three basic models for the shared finances. Separate finances are particularly fair, but also particularly laborious. Every shared expense has to be split, and the lower-earning partner feels every increase in fixed costs much more strongly. A completely joint pot is convenient, but it mixes assets that should remain legally separate and means that every individual purchase needs explaining. The **three-account model** is a compromise that works well in most households. It provides for a joint account for everything shared and two personal accounts for everything else.

The split ratio matters more than the account structure. An equal split seems fair, but with unequal incomes it is not. The lower-earning partner is then left with a much smaller share of their own net income to spend freely, and therefore with a lower savings rate. A split according to income share puts both on an equal footing, because each contributes the same share of their net income.

Partner A has $3,600 net a month, partner B $5,400. The shared fixed costs for rent, utilities, insurance and groceries come to $3,000 a month.

With an equal split, each pays $1,500. A keeps $2,100, B keeps $3,900. A thus contributes 41.7% of their own net income to the shared pot, B only 27.8%.

With a split according to income share, A provides 40% of household income and pays $1,200, while B provides 60% and pays $1,800. Both contribute 33.3% of their net income, and both are left with the same percentage of headroom.

Compared with the equal split, A therefore has $300 a month more and B $300 less. Over ten years, this shifts $36,000 of saving capacity, even though the household spends the same amount overall.

bloecke.titel: Joint accounts, gifts and separate property
bloecke.md:
Paying money into a joint bank account is generally not yet a completed gift; it becomes one when the other partner withdraws money for their own benefit. Putting a house or a brokerage account into joint names, by contrast, is usually a gift of half. Between spouses who are US citizens, gifts are unlimited and tax-free (marital deduction). For gifts to a spouse who is not a US citizen, a higher but limited annual exclusion applies instead ($190,000 in 2025). For unmarried partners, gifts above the annual exclusion of $19,000 per person (2026) must be reported on Form 709, although tax is only due once the lifetime exemption has been used up.

For married couples, the more practical risk is divorce law: an inheritance or money from before the marriage that is mixed into a joint account can lose its status as separate property. Large individual sums therefore belong in an individual account, and the ongoing housekeeping money in the joint account.

## Marital property and prenuptial agreements

Marital property law is state law. Nine states are **community property** states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin, and a few others allow couples to opt in. There, income earned and assets acquired during the marriage belong to both spouses in equal halves, regardless of whose name is on the account. Property owned before the marriage and gifts and inheritances received by one spouse remain separate property. The other states follow the common-law system: each spouse owns what is in their name, and on divorce the court divides marital property by **equitable distribution**, that is, fairly but not necessarily equally.

Retirement savings are often the largest item in a divorce. A 401(k) or pension is divided through a qualified domestic relations order (QDRO), an IRA through a transfer incident to divorce. Social Security has its own protection: a spouse can receive a spousal benefit of up to half of the other's full retirement benefit, and after a marriage of at least ten years this also applies to a divorced spouse, without reducing the ex-partner's benefit. If one partner takes a career break for the children, these claims are often worth more than the portfolio.

A prenuptial agreement has nothing to do with mistrust. It serves to regulate situations that the default law reflects poorly, for example a business that should not be broken up, very unequal starting wealth or second marriages with children from the first marriage. To hold up in court, it usually requires full financial disclosure, enough time before the wedding and ideally a separate lawyer for each partner.

bloecke.md: Under state intestacy law, an unmarried partner inherits nothing, not even after thirty years together, unless the state recognizes a registered domestic partnership or civil union that you have entered into. Without a will, trust or beneficiary designation, the assets go to the deceased's children, parents or siblings. The federal estate tax treats unmarried partners like anyone else: there is no unlimited marital deduction, but the same lifetime exemption. Some of the few states with an inheritance tax, however, tax unrelated heirs at their highest rates, Pennsylvania for example at 15%.

## Estate tax and gift tax

The federal estate tax and gift tax form one unified system. Unlike in many other countries, the tax is owed by the estate or the giver, not by the recipient, and the family relationship matters only for spouses and charities. Every person has a **lifetime exemption** that covers gifts during life and the estate at death together. Under the 2025 tax law, it is $15 million per person for 2026 and will be adjusted for inflation in later years. The rate on amounts above it is 40%. Gifts and bequests to a spouse who is a US citizen are unlimited and tax-free. If the first spouse to die does not use their full exemption, the survivor can take over the unused part (portability), but only if an estate tax return (Form 706) is filed on time, even when no tax is due.

As a result, the federal estate tax affects only very large estates. For most families, other things matter more: about a dozen states and the District of Columbia levy their own estate tax, some with much lower exemptions, such as Massachusetts at $2 million and Oregon at $1 million, and a few states levy an inheritance tax on recipients. Above all, the income tax treatment of inherited assets matters, as shown below.

bloecke.md:
Gifts above the annual exclusion do not cost tax at first. You report them on Form 709, and they reduce the lifetime exemption that remains for your estate. Gifts for education have a special rule: contributions to a 529 plan can be spread over five years by an election on Form 709, so one donor can contribute up to $95,000 ($190,000 for a couple) at once in 2026 without using any of the lifetime exemption, provided they make no further gifts to the same child in those five years.

Because the 40% rate in practice applies to the entire amount above the exemption, the calculation is simple. An estate of $20 million owes 40% of $5 million, that is, $2 million, if no taxable gifts were made during life and no deductions apply.

bloecke.md:
For most families, the income tax is more important than the estate tax. Assets that are inherited receive a new cost basis equal to their market value on the date of death (26 U.S.C. § 1014). The gain built up during the deceased's lifetime is therefore never taxed. Assets received as a gift during life, by contrast, keep the donor's original basis (26 U.S.C. § 1015), and the recipient pays capital gains tax on the entire gain when selling. In community property states, both halves of community property receive the step-up when the first spouse dies.

The step-up does not apply to traditional IRAs and 401(k) accounts. Their beneficiaries pay income tax on withdrawals, and most beneficiaries other than a spouse must empty an inherited account within ten years.

## The annual exclusion over many years

Starting gifts early is the simplest way to move money to the next generation without paperwork. The annual exclusion renews every calendar year and applies per donor and per recipient. Two parents can therefore give each child $38,000 a year without filing a gift tax return. Annual exclusions that are not used in a year cannot be made up later. For estates far below the lifetime exemption, this is mainly a question of timing and control rather than of federal tax; it becomes relevant for very large estates and in states with an estate tax. When giving, the step-up in basis has to be considered: cash or assets with little unrealized gain are better suited for gifts than shares that have risen a lot.

bloecke.titel: Example: gift or inheritance of appreciated shares
bloecke.md:
A mother bought shares for $100,000 decades ago; today they are worth $500,000. Her estate is far below the federal exemption.

If she **gives** the shares to her son during her lifetime, he takes over her basis of $100,000. If he sells, he realizes a long-term gain of $400,000. At a federal rate of 15%, that is $60,000 in tax; if the gain falls into the 20% bracket and the 3.8% net investment income tax applies, it is up to $95,200, plus any state tax.

If the son **inherits** the shares instead, his basis is $500,000. If he sells shortly afterwards, there is practically no gain and no tax. Neither variant triggers federal gift or estate tax.

The difference of $60,000 or more arises solely from the timing. Shares with large gains are usually better kept until death, while cash is better suited for gifts during life.

bloecke.titel: Common mistakes with wills and beneficiaries
bloecke.md:
- Formal requirements are set by state law. A typed will usually has to be signed in front of two witnesses. Handwritten wills without witnesses are recognized only in some states. A self-proving affidavit before a notary speeds up probate.
- Beneficiary designations and account titles take precedence over the will. A 401(k), an IRA, life insurance, payable-on-death and transfer-on-death accounts and joint accounts with right of survivorship pass to the named person, whatever the will says. Under federal law, the spouse is the automatic beneficiary of a 401(k) unless they have waived this in writing in front of a notary or plan representative.
- After a divorce, update the beneficiary forms. Many states automatically revoke designations of a former spouse, but for employer plans federal law can override these state rules; the Supreme Court decided this in Egelhoff v. Egelhoff (2001), and the ex-spouse received the money.
- A spouse can generally not be disinherited completely. In common-law states the surviving spouse has an elective share, often around a third of the estate, and in community property states already owns half of the community property. Children, by contrast, can be disinherited in every state except Louisiana, which retains a limited forced share.
- Parents of minor children should name a guardian in their will. Otherwise a court decides who raises the children.

## Saving for children

An account in the child's name under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act or the Uniform Gifts to Minors Act (UTMA or UGMA account) is an irrevocable gift. The parents manage it as custodians and may only use the money for the child's benefit, not for their own purposes. When the child reaches the age set by state law, usually 18 or 21, the child alone has control over it. The tax advantage is limited by the kiddie tax: in 2025, the first $1,350 of a child's investment income was tax-free and the next $1,350 was taxed at the child's rate; anything above $2,700 is taxed at the parents' [[Marginal tax rate|marginal tax rate]].

For education, a **529 plan** is usually the better tool. The account belongs to the parent, earnings grow tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified education expenses are tax-free. The beneficiary can be changed to another family member, and after 15 years up to $35,000 in total can be rolled over into the beneficiary's Roth IRA, subject to the annual contribution limits. If the child has earned income, for example from a summer job, a custodial Roth IRA is also possible.

bloecke.titel: Three drawbacks of a custodial account
bloecke.md:
In the federal financial aid formula (FAFSA), assets owned by the student count much more heavily than those of the parents: up to 20% of the student's assets, but at most 5.64% of the parents' assets, are expected to be used each year. A custodial account can therefore noticeably reduce need-based aid.

For a child with a disability, own assets can endanger means-tested benefits such as Supplemental Security Income and Medicaid. In this case, an ABLE account or a special needs trust is the more suitable tool.

At 18 or 21, the child decides alone. Parents who want the money earmarked for education or housing then no longer have any legal means of ensuring this.

The 2025 tax law (Public Law 119-21) created a new type of tax-advantaged savings account for children, officially called Trump accounts (26 U.S.C. § 530A). For US citizen children born from 2025 through 2028, the federal government is to pay a one-time $1,000 into the account. Parents, relatives and others can contribute up to $5,000 a year in total, and employers can contribute up to $2,500 a year tax-free for an employee's child. The money must be invested in low-cost funds that track the US stock market, and withdrawals are generally not possible before the year in which the child turns 18; after that, rules similar to those of an IRA apply. Contributions have been possible since July 2026. In an illustrative calculation in which only the $1,000 is invested for 60 years and earns 5% a year, the result is around $18,700. Because the accounts are new, you should check the current IRS guidance before opening one.

## Planning for incapacity

The most common and most expensive misconception in this chapter concerns the case where someone becomes incapable of acting during their lifetime. Many people believe that their spouse may, as a matter of course, decide for them in an emergency. For medical decisions, many states do have default surrogate laws that allow a spouse, adult children or parents to consent to treatment when no healthcare agent has been named; the order and scope differ by state. For money, there is no such rule. Without a **durable power of attorney**, which remains valid after you lose capacity, a spouse cannot manage your individual accounts, sell your car or deal with your retirement accounts. Then a court has to appoint a guardian or conservator, which is public, takes time and costs money, and the court may appoint someone other than the person you would have chosen.

schritte.text: It determines who may act on your behalf with banks, brokers and government agencies. It is usually signed before a notary; ask your bank and broker whether they accept it or require their own form.

schritte.titel: Healthcare power of attorney and living will
schritte.text: The healthcare power of attorney names who decides on medical treatment; the living will states which treatment you want in specific situations. Many states provide their own forms with witness or notary requirements. A HIPAA authorization lets your agents obtain information from doctors.

schritte.titel: Will with a guardian for minor children
schritte.text: It determines who inherits what is not covered by beneficiary designations, who the executor is and who should raise your minor children. A revocable living trust can additionally avoid probate, especially for real estate in several states.

Review the beneficiaries of your 401(k), IRA, life insurance and bank and brokerage accounts after every marriage, divorce and birth, and add payable-on-death or transfer-on-death designations where suitable.

It contains one page per area: bank and brokerage accounts with institution and number, ongoing contracts, insurance policies, digital logins and the location of the will and powers of attorney. Without this list, relatives search for months.

bloecke.md: Powers of attorney, the healthcare directive and the beneficiary forms come first, because they cost little and take effect immediately. Next comes the split ratio in the day-to-day household, because it shifts money every month. After that, it is the turn of the will and of planning gifts and children's accounts, as they need years of lead time. The annual exclusion only helps for the years in which it is used.

All figures in this lesson reflect federal law in 2026 and describe model cases; the rules on marital property, intestacy, wills and state taxes differ from state to state. With real estate in several states, a business, a spouse who is not a US citizen, blended families or very large estates, the situation quickly becomes so complex that an estate planning attorney costs less than a mistake. In addition, tax optimisation is not the top priority. Leaving everything to the surviving spouse can be the right choice even if it costs the children a few advantages, because the survivor would otherwise have to deal with their own children over the house. The calculation allows the decision to be made consciously instead of being based on the tax burden alone.
